articles.title: History and leadership
articles.content: HISTORY is never linear or monolithic. It may progress in leaps and bounds, or falter and regress. It may appear calm and seamless, but be restive and roiling beneath the surface. No wonder, a small trigger can lead to a cataclysm. Historians have long debated whether historical dialectics shape human destiny, or human agency lights up the darkest epochs of history. There’s no definite answer as yet. But there is a broad consensus among them on two requisites of a historical ‘development’ — ripe ‘objective’ conditions, and an intelligent leadership that can transform a conducive environment into, at the very least, meaningful change. Interestingly, the modern era manifests both trends. We see countries and societies long affected by broken governance, endemic corruption, political instability, economic meltdown, civil strife, and regional and global conflagrations. Significant parts of the Middle East, North Africa, and South and West Asia are a dismal reflection of failed or failing states ruled by autocrats or absolutist dynasties — largely without popular mandate and without accountability. Yet there are countries once dismissed as ‘basket-cases’ that have turned themselves around — such asSingapore, Malaysia, Vietnam, Turkiye, South Korea, and China. Over the years, they have taken tremendous strides in terms of political stability, socioeconomic progress, scientific and technological advancement, and human-resource development. They have carved out a large share for themselves in international supply chains and productivity. Much of the credit for their phenomenal achievements goes to their visionary, upright, and courageous political and institutional leadership. True, some of them did not begin as ideal democracies. Yet they built robust, efficient institutions, along with enabling infrastructure, to ensure continuity, stability, peace, and development, and to facilitate a gradual transition to democracy. In contrast, our state has been stuck in a time warp for decades. Every generation has suffered gross ‘elite capture’ characterised by authoritarianism, disenfranchisement, misgovernance, instability, inequality, impoverishment, and never-ending conflicts. In dialectical terms, although the objective conditions for radical sociopolitical change have long been ripe, the desired agency of change — the political and institutional leadership — has remained elusive. No wonder the state continues to exist and function in colonial and neocolonial moulds. Authoritarian governance, a compromised and complex legal order, an extractive and iniquitous social structure, the dominance of the security and administrative apparatuses, and a pro-elite neoliberal policy framework remain among its key features. Our state has been stuck in a time warp for decades. But has this state worked? Never. The founding ideal of a democratic republic itself has been upended. Instead, a security and administrative juggernaut has been forged on the pretext of guarding national security and ‘ideology’. In fact, the state has been virtually detached from its constitutional and democratic controls. It seeks to draw its power, legitimacy, and even sustenance not from the people’s mandate, but from its coercive powers and capacity to control. Hence, it does not need to worry about citizens’ rights or welfare. However, this mindset has drawn an ever-widening wedge between the state — controlled and exploited by a small club of security, bureaucratic, political, landed, industrial, and financial elites — and the people, more than half of whom are classified as ‘poor’ or ‘very poor’. Yet, instead of correcting this perilous course, already scarce resources are being further drained for security obligations — arguably, not so much at home as abroad. This raises a disturbing question: for how long can this behemoth, guided by colonial notions of governance and built around failed politico-legal machinery, sustain itself on the proverbial feet of clay — an ever-brittle economy compounded by worsening security and governance failure? This question has arisen in every post-colonial state where elites have captured power, stolen resources, disenfranchised people, and eventually pushed society into chaos and conflict. But in many instances, upright, visionary, and courageous leadership provided the answers — convincingly — by steering the country out of the woods. Do we have such leadership that can also provide convincing answers — by transforming public angst and alienation towards dysfunctional state structures into a force for building state and political institutions that are democratic, equitable, accountable, and, especially, peace-loving? Ironically, much of the mainstream political leadership — the PPP, PML-N, PTI, and others — has long forsaken its distinct agenda, and even its identity. Rhetoric aside, they have offered little in the way of ‘answers’ to the many problems afflicting the state and governance. Instead, over the decades, they have tended to outrun one another in their efforts to be more ‘compatible’ with the demands of an extractive state toeing the colonial model. The PPP-PML-N duo’s joining hands with non-political elements toweaken the judiciary, election commission, and media, and the PTI’s eagerness to mend fences with the powers that be instead of the release of its leader are some recent instances of crass political opportunism and historical compromises on the part of our ‘popular’ leaders. So, the causes of our recurrent sociopolitical tragedies and the decline of democracy should not be traced to history’s apathy in the face of ominous lengthening shadows. It is the frayed moral fabric of much of our leadership — political and institutional — that gives preference to personal, political, and institutional interests over democracy and the good of the people — the real masters. Under these hopeless circumstances, a new class of self-led movers of history — a sort of Gen-Z — is needed to change our collective destiny.
articles.author: Shahab Usto

articles.title: External sector turning points
articles.content: THEslight increasein workers’ remittances reported for October prompted a host of questions directed to me. Here are the responses. The rise is too small to matter. In fact, it falls far short of what it needs to be to serve its purpose: helping plug the trade deficit. There is no reason in the world for celebration based on one data outturn. What matters is the trend that a series of data points describe; most often, that trend is intelligible only when seen in its proper context. So what is the proper context for remittances? First, remittances are traditionally how Pakistan’s economy finances its trade deficits. The trend is cyclical and reveals itself when you take a 12-month average of the total trade balance plus remittances, then plot that on a month-to-month basis. You will notice something. A wavy line emerges. From a low point in 2015, it rises slowly until it briefly turns positive — around $40 million — in November 2015. Then it plunges back below the X-axis, before bottoming out in July 2018 at around negative $1.45 billion. This is trade balance plus remittances, mind you, so a negative value means remittances can’t plug the trade deficit, and the balance is being financed from reserves or borrowing. If you don’t see the reserves plunging by the same amount in that month, then you can be sure the balance is being financed by new borrowing, and that data will show up in the balance-of-payments whenever the next release comes along. From July 2018, the line rises sharply again until it hits a fresh peak in November 2020 at around $100m. It then plunges again until it hits its second trough in July 2022 at negative $1.14bn. This is when another attempt to stabilise Pakistan’s economy by choking its imports began — abortively, as it turned out. At least since June, the trade deficit’s growth has outstripped remittances. After that, the next peak — $780m — was in March 2025; it has stayed above the X-axis for the most part, barring one or two months. But if the trend so far is anything to go by, the line has been falling since March, reaching $480m by September. This is the 12-month average. For September alone, the figure is closer to $150m. The October trade data has not yet been released, so we don’t know where the figure will be for that month. But given the pace of increase in imports, and the relative stagnation of export growth, grounds for excess optimism are conspicuous by their absence. This is entirely in sync with the long-run trend of how Pakistan’s external sector behaves. It heaves and ebbs in cycles. Take the earliest low point of the trade deficit in some month and trace it forward. What you see is the trade deficit growing as imports outstrip exports each month, but remittances cover the gap. Hence, the overall current account in the balance of payments remains above zero. Then the trade deficit starts to grow beyond the ability of the remittances to cover. The current account falls into deficit. Borrowing increases during these months to cover the deficit. As the required pace of borrowing increases, the government is unable to fetch dollars in quantities sufficient to pay for the deficit, and the reserves start to fall. Once that fall begins, it becomes very difficult to contain the situation. Eventually, the reserves drop to a level that necessitates a return to the IMF for a bailout. That bailout requires taking steps to choke imports and kill the fiscal deficit as well, and eventually normalcy returns, but at the cost of choking economic activity in the country. Take four indicators and plot them from 2014 onwards (you can start earlier if you like). Plot exports, imports, remittances, and external payment obligations over a 12-month period from that year onward. For external obligations, use the total figure for “predetermined drains” given in the International Liquidity sheet released every month by the State Bank. What you’ll see is that exports are the slowest to grow over the years, while external obligations are the fastest. Here is what the numbers look like: exports have grown by 1.4x since 2014, imports by 1.6x, remittances by 2.7x, and external obligations by 4.6x. This is the real long-run trend that needs to break before any indicator can mean anything. This year alone, for example, the trade deficit has grown faster than remittances. There are a few different ways to measure this growth, and each gives you slightly different numbers. But all of them show that, at least since June, the trade deficit’s growth has outstripped remittances. If this trend continues, then it shows we have already passed the peak that historically defines the turning point from growth to bust. And there is little reason today to believe that the trend will turn around on its own. In past periods, governments had a story to tell at this point, even if the story held little water. In both past peaks, when the trade deficit began yawning and eating up all current inflows, both governments in power at each peak said their period had seen a large inflow of machinery that, once installed, would lead to export growth and reverse the trend. That story failed to pan out both times. But at least it was there. What is the story now? What is this government’s plan for containing the trade deficit, which is only a few months away from outstripping remittances’ ability to plug it? The only story they’re running with these days is some urgency to see dramatic improvements in the country’s credit rating by June 2027. What is that in preparation for? More borrowing? If so, then welcome to the old world. The writer is a business and economy journalist.
articles.author: Khurram Husain

articles.title: The unmaking of…
articles.content: AMERICAN WASPs have lost their sting. The recent US midterm elections results are balm to the pain felt after Donald Trump’s return to the White House two years ago. This November, that surge of fickle popularity changed allegiance from a Republican red to a Democratic blue. Almost overnight, individual candidates emerging from among the leaderless Democrat Party have wrested control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. It was a triumph of right over might, or as its newest star — Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed from Michigan — put it, the victory of “the many over money”. Investment in the 2026 midterms has been unprecedented. The final amount is expected to exceed $12 billion, which will be around 30 per cent more than that spent in 2022, and vastly more than the meagre $2bn spent in 2002. Inflation has little to do with it. This year, the top 40 donors contributed $2.5bn, led by the trillionaire Elon Musk. He squandered about $500 million supporting Republican candidates. There is no Theodore H. White alive to chronicle this electoral extravagance. His book — The Making of the President 1960 — provided a narrative of the rise of the charismatic John F. Kennedy. Unlike Abdul El-Sayed, Kennedy did not have to fight big money. Kennedy’s father was already a millionaire. But, like El-Sayed (a Muslim), Kennedy (a Roman Catholic) had to overcome bitter religious prejudice. The midterm results were a triumph of right over might. In September 1960, Kennedy delivered a well-aimed rejoinder to critics who ‘obscured’ the campaign by questioning his loyalty. He asserted that “the separation of church and state” was absolute. He went further: “I believe in an America that is officially neither Catholic, Protestant, nor Jewish.” He contended that allegiance in America was to the constitution, adding that “no man should be denied public office merely because his religion differs from the president’s”. The real issues, Kennedy argued, were not his religious faith but hungry children, old people unable to pay medical bills, struggling farmers, insufficient schools, slums, etc. Almost 70 years later, Abdul El-Sayed based his platform on the same issues — schools, healthcare, the cost of groceries, and fuel prices. El-Sayed owes more, though, to his prototype Barack Hussein Obama. He too was criticised for being a “little bit young, a little bit brown, a little bit Muslim”. Barack Obama was 47 years old when elected president; El-Sayed has just begun his 43rd year. He will be 45 in 2028, when he will foreseeably make his first bid for the presidency. By then, he will have enough credentials. He will have prompted Trump to end the Israel-incited Iran war and caused a rethink of America’s relationship with Israel. His views on Israel are even-handed: “I believe in equal rights, to peace, dignity, and self-determination for Palestinians and Jewish Israelis alike.” He draws a line between Israel and Zionism and he deplores the use of US tax dollars to fund genocide in Gaza, or anywhere else. Like Obama, El-Sayed is master of the media. He began early. His valedictorian address in 2007 at Michigan University impressed president Bill Clinton enough to earn this compliment: “I wish every person in the world who […] cannot reach across the religious divides, could have heard you speak today.” Clinton advised Abdul El-Sayed to go into politics, despite the burden of his name. Today, media is not only king; it is the sceptre of presidents. Theodore White analysed that “once Gutenberg put the Bible in print, neither church nor prince could maintain authority [.] Television reached a world that even if it could not read, it could look”. But he warned that, while a president “might control camera attention, he could not control events”. Many will remember the slogan that pursued Lyndon B. Johnson over that other undeclared war, in Vietnam: “Hey, hey, LBJ! How many kids did you kill today?” How will Abdul El-Sayed position himself vis-à-vis Pakistan, as a senator-elect and a president-in-waiting? Obama visited Pakistan as a student for three weeks in 1981. He learned how to cook local dishes like qeema and dal. He carried away from Pakistan nothing more than recipes and a “changed perspective on economic disparity”. Abdul El-Sayed has not yet visited Pakistan. Frequently addressing Pakistanis in America, he has called out strongly “for human rights and democratic governance”, drawing a parallel with Egypt (the home of his parents). He cited “its history of military dictatorship” and argued that “neither government should be shielded from criticism, or receive US aid, simply because they are US allies”. Will Trump and his coterie learn from the results of the US midterm elections? Will they soften in the face of reality, or become increasingly defiant in defeat?
articles.author: F.S. Aijazuddin

articles.title: Forex crowding out
articles.content: THE State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) has successfullyrebuiltforeign exchange reserves over the last three years. Much of this success, however, has been purchased by drawing liquidity directly out of the forex market. It attributes its purchases to improved market liquidity and describes their purpose as strengthening external buffers and the capacity to meet external obligations. These are legitimate considerations. Yet the extent to which dollars have been siphoned from the market to accumulate reserves raises concerns for the wider economy. When the central bank becomes a persistent and dominant buyer of dollars in the market, it effectively crowds out some private businesses, which must compete with an institution that enjoys an informational advantage. While Pakistan is familiar with the crowding out of the private sector through large and persistent governmentborrowingto finance budget deficits, crowding out in the foreign exchange market is unprecedented. If the forex market has sufficient depth, it can smoothly accommodate both the central bank’s purchases and the private sector’s requirements. But where the market is constrained, the adjustment has to take place somewhere. It may appear in the exchange rate, transaction spreads, delays in opening letters of credit (LCs), or restrictions on access to foreign currency. In effect, private sector buyers are either priced out of the market or pushed into waiting queues. There have been several media reports of import payment delays and dollar rationing by some banks. Concerns about these practices have also surfaced in official trade assessments. TheUS National Trade Estimate Report 2026, for instance, records stakeholder concerns about delays in banks’ issuance of LCs, reportedly resulting from informal SBP limitations on commercial banks’ borrowing of foreign currency through the interbank market. The report also highlights that corporations and foreign equity holders have encountered administrative delays, documentation hurdles, and informal queuing systems when seeking to repatriate their profits, dividends, and royalties in dollars. The SBP must reassess its market interventions. Such restrictions carry consequences. Central banking, in essence, is not an accounting exercise and balance sheet management. Every action has microeconomic and macroeconomic repercussions for resource allocation, business costs, investment decisions, and, ultimately, economic growth. Thus, a policy intended to strengthen the country’s external position can, paradoxically, undermine investors’ sentiments and the productive capacity to generate future foreign exchange. A further paradox concerns theexchange ratesignal. Despite extensive purchases, the exchange rate is not responding. Conventional macroeconomic models offer limited help in explaining such interventions. Instead, an exchange rate microstructure approach, built on order flow, may offer a better explanation of exchange rate determination. Order flow refers to the buying and selling pressure generated by market participants. This approach recognises the importance of participants’ identities, information and trading behaviour in influencing exchange rate movements. A study by Evans and Lyons, published in the Journal of Political Economy in 2002, shows that order flow has substantial explanatory power for exchange rate changes. When a central bank, which also issues licences to the market participants, enters the market, its order flow may convey its preferences about price as well as quantity. Forex dealers, observing this institutional order flow, may adjust their quotes and inventory positions accordingly. Consequently, the exchange rate may increasingly reflect the central bank’s institutional preferences rather than the underlying balance of forex demand and supply. Granular level data can explain forex dynamics on the basis of the order flow model. The SBP has both the technical capacity and the high-frequency data required for such analysis. It could examine import payment delays, outstanding foreign exchange requests, transaction spreads, interbank turnover, and the daily pattern of its own purchases. A range of forex market data is already covered by IMF monitoring and reporting requirements on a daily basis. Greater transparency and wider dissemination of this data may also allow independent researchers to apply an order flow model to exchange rate formation in Pakistan. Reserve accumulation is a necessary but not sufficient condition for stability, which ultimately depends on the economy’s ability to generate foreign exchange through exports, investment, and productive activity. The SBP must, therefore, assess its market interventions within a robust analytical framework and develop an exit strategy for its dollar purchases for reserve accumulation.
articles.author: Farooq Arby

articles.title: Iran status quo
articles.content: THE current ‘no war, no peace’ situation in the US-Iran conflict is unsustainable. While the immediate fear of a new US-Israeli strike on Iran — and a greater regional conflagration — may have passed, thanks mainly to thedrubbingthe Republicans received in the American midterm elections, the Gulf will not return to normal unless there is stable long-term peace. True to form, President Donald Trump has been oscillating between claiming that more attacks are not needed and issuing new threats. After talking to the Qatari prime minister, he said that the US would maintain the “status quo” vis-à-vis Iran, while his secretary of state has asserted that economic pressure on Tehran will continue. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, meanwhile, has slammed America’s “diplomacy through threats”. The fact is that the US and Israel have failed to subdue Iran on the battlefield, and while the economic sanctions are hurting the Iranians, there are few signs that the pressure will make them yield to America. If anything, the feeling in Tehran is that if Iran is made to endure economic pain, the entire region, and in fact the wider international community, will feel it as well, as the overeight-month blockade of the Strait of Hormuzhas shown. The Iranians have said their seven-point proposal is on the table if the Americans want to consider it, though the US has termed these conditions “absurd”. The US status quo is unlikely to hold, and may, in fact, further inflame matters, which is why Washington’s energies should be directed towards a negotiated settlement. As American academic John Mearsheimer told the Margalla Dialogue in Islamabad on Tuesday, “there is no way the US can defeat Iran”. For the sake of peace in the region and for global economic stability, the status quo needs to end, and give way to a sustainable peace. The US cannot hold the world hostage in order to find an honourable exit from a disastrous war for which it has only itself — and Israel — to blame. Iran’s demands may appear maximalist at the moment, but if Tehran is approached with respect, and given guarantees of no more attacks, it may soften its approach. The American people have made their displeasure with Mr Trump’s war clear in the midterms. Instead of dragging this matter on, he should find ways to quickly wrap things up. Israel is obviously unhappy about any cessation of hostilities; as per the Israeli media Mr Trump and the Zionist state’s prime minister had a tense phone call on the matter recently. The US leader should remember that it was questionable Israeli advice that got him into this predicament. He would be better off ignoring Tel Aviv’s toxic persuasion, and working with regional states to find a solution to permanently end hostilities with Iran.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Unspent funds
articles.content: THE slow pace of development spending shows how public investment continues to bear the brunt of efforts to create a primary fiscal surplus, while wasteful government expenditure remains largely protected. The numbers speak for themselves. The government spent just 10.4pc of the Rs1tr PSDP allocation during the first four months of the current year. Even against the Rs412.3bn authorised for spending, actual utilisation remained exceptionally low. Several ministries could not spend even a single rupee. This pattern is hardly new. Successive governments have routinely sacrificed development spending to meet fiscal targets, particularly under IMF programmes. The lender’s strict conditions on fiscal deficits and primary balances leave little room for development works. They find it easier to delay development than to confront politically influential lobbies, reduce administrative waste, or cut their own privileges. Public investment becomes the easiest adjustment whenever revenues fall short. The current figures, however, should not be mistaken for the final spending position. Disbursements are likely to accelerate as the fiscal year progresses, particularly towards its closing months. Such hurried spending reflects poor planning and weak project preparation. Governments announce ambitious development allocations for political reasons without ensuring that projects are ready for implementation. The result is a rush to spend towards the end of the year, often at the expense of quality and value for money. The underlying problem is equally clear. The government has failed to broaden the tax base and raise the tax-to-GDP ratio, which has for long hovered around 10pc or lower. Without a stronger revenue base, there is little money available for development. The burden of financing the state continues to fall on a relatively narrow segment of taxpayers, while large sections of the economy remain outside the tax net. A fiscal surplus has little meaning if it is achieved by starving the economy of investment. Public infrastructure is essential for raising productivity and improving living standards. Its neglect creates higher costs for future generations. The government must raise more revenue by broadening the tax net. It must also examine its own non-development expenditure and cut wasteful spending. The country needs a revenue system capable of financing growth, not one that repeatedly makes investment its first casualty.
